rewritten_text:
What's wrong?”

I said:

“Dad, and Mum, and my sister, and—”

Then I broke down crying. He said:

“Oh, darn it, don't get so upset. We all have our troubles, and this one will turn out all right. What's happened to them?”

“They're—they're—are you the boat's watchman?”

“Yes,” he said, sounding quite pleased with himself. “I'm the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and chief deckhand. Sometimes I'm the cargo and the passengers too. I'm not as rich as old Jim Hornback. I can't afford to be so generous to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, throwing money around like he does. But I've told him plenty of times I wouldn't trade places with him. A sailor's life is the life for me, I said. I'd be damned before I'd live two miles outside town, where nothing ever happens, even for all his money and as much again. I said—”

I interrupted him:

“They're in terrible trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Dad and Mum and my sister and Miss Hooker. If you'd take your ferry up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Well, there's only one.”

“What—you don't mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good heavens! What on earth are they doing there?”

“Well, they didn't go there on purpose.”

“I should think not! Good Lord, they haven't got a chance unless they get off quick! How on earth did they get into a mess like that?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting the town upriver—”

“Yes, Booth's Landing. Go on.”

“She was visiting Booth's Landing, and just as evening began she set off across the river with her black servant woman in the horse ferry. She was going to spend the night at her friend's house, Miss What's-her-name—I can't remember. They lost their steering oar, swung round, and drifted downstream backwards for about two miles. Then they crashed against the wreck and got folded over it. The ferryman, the black woman, and the horses all drowned, but Miss Hooker caught hold and pulled herself onto the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we came downstream in our flat-bottomed trading boat. We couldn't see the wreck in the darkness until we were right on it, and our boat got folded over it too. Everyone survived except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the kindest soul! I almost wish it had been me instead, I do.”

“By George! I've never heard anything to beat that.

“Just a tick.”

“Where'd you find it?”

“In the woods.”

“What do you want for it?”

“I don't know. I don't want to sell it.”

“Fine. It's a pretty small tick, anyway.”

“Anyone can criticize a tick that doesn't belong to them. I'm happy with it. It's good enough for me.”

“Oh, come on, there are ticks everywhere. I could have a thousand if I wanted.”

“So why don't you? Because you know perfectly well you can't. This one's pretty early in the season, I'd say. It's the first I've seen this year.”

“Hey, Huck—I'll give you my tooth for it.”

“Let me see.”

Tom took out a piece of paper and carefully unwrapped it. Huckleberry examined the tooth with longing. The temptation was almost irresistible. Finally he asked:

“Is it real?”

Tom pulled up his lip and displayed the gap.

“All right, then,” said Huckleberry. “It's a deal.”

Tom put the tick in the percussion-cap box that had recently held the pinchbug captive, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer.

When Tom arrived at the little wooden schoolhouse standing on its own, he strode briskly inside, looking like someone who had honestly hurried to get there. He hung his hat on a peg and threw himself into his seat with purposeful energy. The teacher, enthroned above the class in his large armchair with its woven wood-strip seat, was dozing to the sleepy hum of lessons. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that hearing his full name meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to seek refuge in a lie when he noticed two long blond braids hanging down a back that he recognized with love's electric instinct. Beside that figure was the only empty seat on the girls' side of the schoolhouse. He answered at once:

“I stopped to talk to Huckleberry Finn!”

The teacher's heart seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The murmur of lessons fell silent. The students wondered whether this reckless boy had lost his mind. The teacher said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk to Huckleberry Finn.”

There could be no misunderstanding him.

“Thomas Sawyer, that is the most astonishing confession I've ever heard. A mere stroke of the punishment ruler won't do for this offence. Take off your jacket.”

The teacher worked his arm until it tired and his supply of thin whipping branches had noticeably decreased. Then he issued his command:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! Let this be a warning.”

The giggles spreading around the room seemed to embarrass Tom. In fact, his confusion owed more to his worshipful awe of the idol whose name he did not know, and the frightening joy of his extraordinary luck.

Sir Walter had rented a very fine house in Camden Place, in an elevated, distinguished location suitable for a man of importance. He and Elizabeth had settled there to their complete satisfaction.

Anne entered with a heavy heart, expecting to feel imprisoned for months. ‘Oh, when will I leave you again?’ she anxiously asked herself. But the unexpected warmth of her welcome cheered her a little. Her father and sister were glad to see her because they could show her the house and furniture, and they greeted her kindly. At dinner, they remarked on the advantage of having her as a fourth person at the table.

Mrs. Clay was pleasant and full of smiles, but Anne had expected her polite attentions. She had always known Mrs. Clay would put on the proper show at her arrival. The friendliness of the other two was a surprise. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and she would soon hear why. They had little interest in hearing her news. First they hinted that she ought to tell them how deeply their old neighbours missed them, which Anne could not honestly do. After a few halfhearted questions, they took over the conversation entirely. Uppercross interested them not at all, and Kellynch very little. Everything was about Bath.

They delighted in assuring her that Bath had exceeded their expectations in every way. Their house was certainly the best in Camden Place. Their drawing rooms had clear advantages over every other room they had seen or heard about. The decorations were equally superior, as was the taste shown in the furniture. Everyone wanted to know them; everyone wished to visit. They had refused many introductions, yet strangers were still constantly leaving visiting cards.

Here was a rich supply of pleasure. Could Anne be surprised that her father and sister were happy? Perhaps she could not, but she had to sigh. Her father felt no loss of dignity in his changed circumstances. He missed neither the duties nor the standing of a landowner living on his estate, and he found so much to boast about in the petty concerns of town life. Then Elizabeth flung open the folding doors and walked triumphantly from one drawing room to the other, praising their size. Anne could only sigh, smile, and marvel that a woman who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall could be proud of the space between two walls perhaps thirty feet apart.

But these were not their only sources of happiness. They also had Mr. Elliot.
